props.title: Real Fiction

sections.content: Real Fiction represents a fascinating experimental approach by Korean director Kim Ki-duk, shot in real-time over 200 minutes but edited down to a tight 86 minutes. The film follows a street artist who embarks on a violent revenge spree through Seoul, with the entire movie captured using multiple cameras simultaneously tracking the action. This groundbreaking approach predates similar real-time experiments like Russian Ark (2002) and Victoria (2015), though with a grittier, more fragmented aesthetic that reflects the psychological state of its protagonist.

sections.content: The film's exploration of violence and revenge themes aligns with other notable Korean works of the period, including Oldboy (2003) and Sympathy for Mr. Vengeance (2002). However, Kim Ki-duk's signature style is more contemplative and experimental, using the real-time format to create a uniquely unsettling atmosphere. The technical achievement is remarkable considering the coordination required across multiple camera crews tracking simultaneous action through Seoul's crowded streets.

The blurring of reality and fiction that gives the film its title manifests both in the story and the filming method itself. Like Birdman (2014) and 1917 (2019), the illusion of continuous time creates a heightened sense of immediacy, though Real Fiction achieves this through actual real-time filming rather than clever editing to disguise cuts. sections.content: While not the first film to experiment with real-time narrative - High Noon (1952) being a famous early example - Real Fiction pushed technical boundaries by coordinating multiple simultaneous camera crews. This approach influenced later works like Silent House (2011) and Lost in London (2017), which similarly embraced the challenges of real-time filming while adding their own innovations.
